cards.title: B2B premiums: tie the gift to the buyer's company, not personal use
cards.summary: In corporate B2B marketing, a discount or company-relevant premium beats a personal-use gift because the buyer is rewarded for being a sharp buyer.
cards.use_when: Designing a bonus or premium for a business buyer, especially a corporate employee who must justify the purchase to management
steps: Recognize the incentive asymmetry: a corporate buyer looks good to management by getting the lowest price, so a larger discount may outperform a free gift intended for personal use.
If you do offer a premium to a business buyer, make it related to the product and valuable to the buyer's company — not to the buyer personally.

Model it on the publisher of high-priced technical journals on CD-ROM that offered a free CD-ROM stacker and reader with a group purchase: high perceived value, tightly tied to the product, and it made the prospect look like a smart buyer.
For lead generation specifically, keep the premium directly related to the product or service. Unrelated high-value premiums bring in freebie seekers and unqualified leads.
Modest premiums directly related to the product or service increase total response and still bring a greater volume of qualified leads, even though some serial freebie seekers will always respond.
caveats: The source's preference for related premiums is stated as personal experience, not a universal law; unrelated high-value premiums can still generate volume if raw lead count is the goal.
A discount-only strategy may train buyers to wait for discounts and can erode margin.

cards.title: Use the premium as a gate for a salesperson visit (Ricoh pattern)
cards.summary: A free report or gift can be conditioned on accepting a demonstration, letting the premium qualify and pull prospects into the sales process.
cards.use_when: Planning a lead-generation campaign where a sales rep must get in front of the prospect before a sale can happen
steps: Lead with a soft offer such as 'send for the free report,' which the source says is the most common use of a related premium.
Tie the premium to a harder next step when you need a meeting: offer the impressive report on the condition that a salesperson hand-delivers it.

Follow the Ricoh model: the mailing offered a small gift as an incentive to reply, then Ricoh called to schedule a demonstration; the gift was delivered personally by the rep only after the demonstration.
This conditions the giveaway on the prospect's time and interest, which filters out pure freebie seekers while still lifting reply rates.
Apply the same structure to ecommerce by gating a high-value guide or sample kit behind a scheduled consultation, demo, or onboarding call when the product needs explanation.
caveats: The gate reduces total responses by design; you are trading volume for qualification.
Delivery must actually happen as promised — a delayed or missing gift damages trust at the worst moment in the sales process.

cards.title: Sample offers: let prospects test your product or service on their own material
cards.summary: A sample offer renders the service or runs the product on the prospect's own input so they can judge fit before buying.
cards.use_when: Selling equipment, software, or a technical service where the buyer must see results on their own data before committing
steps: Frame the offer as rendering the service or letting the customer use the product on a sample basis, either to demonstrate capability or to analyze needs.

Use a concrete customer-supplied input. The pelletizer manufacturer asked prospects to send a five-pound bag of their compound with the desired pellet size; the company ran it and returned the pellets to show quality.
Graver Chemical used the same logic for Ecosorb filtration medium: 'Is Ecosorb right for your application? We'd be delighted to evaluate a water sample.'

For software, demonstrate live on the prospect's problem. When a skeptical buyer asked how long a custom database application would take, the rep built a working prototype against their database in 30 minutes instead of answering — the prospect bought on the spot.
Adapt for ecommerce: offer a free audit, a sample sized to the customer's spec, or a same-day configured demo on their data rather than a generic trial.
caveats: Sample programs carry fulfillment cost and turnaround time; set expectations for how fast you return results.
The source's examples are B2B and service settings — transfer the structure, not the unverified claim that it works identically for consumer ecommerce.

cards.title: Trial and evaluation offers: no-cost use for a set period, no obligation
cards.summary: Let prospects use the product or service free for a specified window with the option to return at your expense or buy at list price.
cards.use_when: Designing a trial for physical equipment, software, or a metered service where usage itself demonstrates value
steps: Define the trial precisely: a specified period, no cost, no obligation to buy. The pelletizer maker shipped the machine for a month at no obligation, then let the prospect return it at the manufacturer's expense or buy it.
For metered services, translate the trial into free usage units: an online database or long-distance service can offer '30 minutes of use free.'

Note the measured framing effect from Jim Kobs' book on two MCI ads: '30 free minutes' of long-distance pulled roughly twice the response of '$5 off' the phone bill because the minutes were perceived as greater value — even though both discount the service.
For product evaluations, phrase it as shipping at no cost for whatever technical evaluation the buyer needs, with the option to return and owe nothing or buy at list price.

Combat trial inertia — prospects who request the product and then never open it — by bundling the trial with a decision incentive: 'If you accept the free trial and buy within 30 days, take 10 percent off.'
Send periodic reminders by mail or phone during the evaluation window to get more prospects to actually try the product and lift lead-to-sale conversion.
caveats: Free trials and evaluations fail through inertia, laziness, or lack of time, not necessarily lack of interest — plan the nudge sequence before launch.
The MCI comparison is a single historical test; verify whether free-unit framing beats a cash discount in your own market with a split test.

cards.title: Loss leaders online: fund a cheap front-end with full affiliate commission
cards.summary: Sell a genuinely valuable product at near or below cost to build a customer list, and use attractive affiliate economics to drive the volume.
cards.use_when: Launching an online information product where the strategic goal is acquiring a large customer list rather than per-unit profit
steps: Create the loss leader as a product with wide appeal across your market, valuable enough that buyers will return to you for more. The source's example is an e-book priced at a $39 list.
Approach affiliates — online marketers you have a commission agreement with — and propose they sell the $39 e-book to their lists at $19, framed as a $20 discount.

Instead of the customary 50 percent commission, offer affiliates 100 percent of the $19 sale. Rationale: 50 percent of $19 is only $9.50, too little to interest them, while 100 percent of $19 equals a 50 percent commission on a $38 sale and gets their attention.
Set the $39 list price so the math works: a $20 customer discount and a $19 affiliate payout both look strong, leaving you the list.

Profit comes afterward by selling the newly acquired customers additional products at regular mark-up, the same pattern coin dealers used by selling an American Silver Eagle at 'our cost' and then pitching a $200 set.
caveats: The coin-dealer numbers (10,000 first orders producing 1,000 sets and $200,000) are an example, not a forecast.
You must give real value at the loss-leader price or customers will not return; the strategy depends on back-end offer quality.
Paying 100 percent commission means the first sale produces no revenue for you — model cash flow accordingly.

cards.title: Place the offer in the copy according to its strength
cards.summary: Strong-but-standard offers belong in the close; unusually generous offers deserve outer-envelope or headline prominence.
cards.use_when: Deciding where in a mailing, ad, or landing page to feature the offer
steps: Always feature the offer prominently on the response device — reply card, order form, or checkout element.
For a strong but standard offer, describe it in the closing section of the promotion, and mention it elsewhere in the copy as appropriate.

The more compelling or unusual the offer, the more prominently feature it. McGraw-Hill's Chemical Engineer's Book Club put an unusually generous free copy of Perry's Handbook on the outer envelope with the teaser asking why they were giving away the 50th Anniversary Edition practically for free.

Leading with the offer in a headline is the exception, not the default — but do it when the offer is particularly powerful, as in 'Develop applications up to 6X faster — guaranteed or your money back,' where the guarantee in the headline answers skepticism about a big promise up front.
In the source's own letter promoting copywriting services, the free Mini-Report is the lead, which generated a 3 percent response on a mailing to a couple hundred newsletter publishers.
caveats: Response figures cited are from the source's own campaigns and its clients' testimonials; treat them as examples, not benchmarks.
An offer-led headline trades product or prospect focus for offer focus — test whether it fits your audience.

cards.title: Focus copywriting effort on the three hot spots
cards.summary: Most copy edits are irrelevant to response; only the positioning-dependent lead sections, the big idea, and the offer copy on the reply element materially move results.
cards.use_when: Allocating limited copywriting and review time across a promotion
steps: Spend little time agonizing over punctuation, grammar, spelling, and minor word choice — the source argues these rarely change response between version A and version B.

Hot spot 1, position-dependent copy: in a #10 direct-mail package the outer envelope teaser plus the sales letter headline and lead; in a magalog the front cover, inside front cover, headline and lead, and back cover; on a landing page the banner, headline, salutation, and lead; in email the subject line and first paragraph.

Hot spot 2, the central message or big idea — how you position the selling proposition. For an energy-stock newsletter, that is the difference between hedging a portfolio against an oil-triggered bear market versus profiting from crude reaching $200 a barrel.

Hot spot 3, the offer copy on the reply element — how the offer itself is expressed. 'Free information kit' usually generates more leads than the vaguer 'send for more information' because a kit feels more tangible and valuable.
On an order form, a single word change matters only when it changes the offer: '$100 a year' versus '$500 a year,' or a 10-day versus 90-day money-back guarantee.
Keep polishing headlines, leads, offer copy, theme, and big idea until you are confident they can work.
caveats: The claim that most copy edits are inconsequential is the source's opinion; regulated, technical, or brand-sensitive copy may still require strict editing.
Hot-spot positions differ by format — map them to your actual channel before rewriting.

cards.title: Reply cards still lift total response, even online
cards.summary: Enclosing a physical reply device signals that a reply is expected and raises response across mail, phone, and web channels.
cards.use_when: Producing a lead-generation or order mailing while worrying that prospects will only respond online or by phone
steps: Keep the reply card in the mailing even if most prospects will not use it — the source disagrees with marketers who omit it in the internet age.
Reason: the card graphically signals that the prospect is supposed to reply, and it lifts total response including phone and online responses, not just mail.

For a lead-generating direct mail, the simplest card has the prospect check which offers they want, fill in contact details, and return it — postage can be required from the prospect or prepaid via business reply.

Add a perforated tear-off stub to the reply card to spotlight the premium with a picture, or let the prospect keep it as an order record with space for date and check number; it can also highlight the guarantee.

For space ads, include a reply coupon in the bottom right corner and specify a right-hand page in the insertion order so it is easy to clip. The source reports this increases response by roughly 10 to 15 percent based on personal experience.
Offer multiple response channels — mail, fax, web, email, and a toll-free phone number — rather than assuming phone or web is preferred.
caveats: The 10–15 percent coupon lift is the author's experience, not a tested benchmark for your audience.
Print-ad coupons are now uncommon; the effect may differ in current media environments.

cards.title: Order device formats: order card, BRE, 8.5x11 form, invoice style
cards.summary: Choose an order device format based on how much selling copy you need and how payment returns.
cards.use_when: Designing the order form or reply element for a direct-mail or mail-order promotion
steps: For an order-generating package, use an order card or form plus a #9 business reply envelope so the recipient can return the order with payment.

The classic reply element in a #10 package was a 4 x 9 inch order card that fit in the BRE without folding; many marketers now use an 8 1/2 x 11 inch order form that folds like a letter for the BRE because it holds more copy.

Try the invoice-style order form: list every feature or benefit as a separate 'item' with a price or value, creating the perception that the prospect is getting a lot for the money. The source notes it is widely used for newsletter and magazine subscriptions, with Kiplinger's as an example.
Note the disagreement on clutter: some marketers swear a busier, more cluttered order form pulls better, while others prefer clean, easy-to-fill forms. Test rather than assume.
For membership, mortgage, insurance, and other applications where qualification matters, design the reply element to look like a membership application or official enrollment form.
caveats: Format preferences are practitioner opinions; the source presents both sides and does not declare a winner.
Larger order forms cost more to print and mail — weigh against expected lift.

cards.title: Stickers, tokens, and the yes/no/maybe offer on the reply device
cards.summary: Physical interactive elements on order forms are a proven response booster, and the yes/no/maybe offer lets undecided prospects reply without committing.
cards.use_when: Adding engagement mechanics to a direct-mail order form or considering a softer response option for hesitant prospects
steps: Use tokens, peel-off stickers, stamp sheets, and similar physical devices on the order form — the source calls them proven response boosters and often neglected.
For multiple products such as magazine subscriptions, print a stamp sheet with each magazine's name and picture; the customer affixes stamps for the titles they want.

Build a yes/no/maybe offer with or without stickers: 'yes' affixes to the order sheet to buy, 'maybe' requests a free trial for the less certain, and 'no' selects the negative offer described elsewhere in the source.
Simpler variants use only yes/no stickers, or just a yes sticker.
The value is that hesitation has a place to go — a 'maybe' reply still captures the prospect and a lead rather than losing them entirely.
caveats: These mechanics assume a physical mail piece; online equivalents require different design.
The source gives no measured lift figures for stickers, only that they are established practice.

cards.title: Nine techniques for response-maximizing order devices
cards.summary: Concrete design moves — premium images, prominent guarantees, roomy forms, key codes, short web forms, AVS copy, and color — that raise reply and order rates.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a reply element or online order form before production or launch
steps: Show a picture of the premium: a photo of merchandise, the front cover of a free special report, or multiple report covers fanned out.
Highlight the guarantee on the order device with a certificate-style border, the owner's signature beneath the copy, and clear legible type.
Leave enough space for name and address; cramped areas cause prospects to give up in frustration.
If you key-code via the mailing label, design the piece so the label returns with the response device — affix or imprint the label on the reply element.

Track phone responses without a unique number per promotion by putting 'Ask for Betty' or 'Ask for Extension 112' after the number and having operators ask callers which extension they want; for web traffic, send each promotion to a unique URL.
Create short, memorable, product-connected domain names like myveryfirstebook.com or beer.com, which get more traffic than long names without a logical connection.

On web lead forms, ask the minimum qualifying questions. DM News (10/20/08) reported roughly 20 percent of visitors abandon the form per field or question presented; consumer forms usually need only name and email, B2B may add company and phone, and if the sales process requires an inbound call, phone is mandatory.
For ecommerce order pages, add copy reminding the customer that the name entered must match the name on the credit card exactly, to reduce AVS mismatches and rejected-card complaints.

Test color rather than assuming: in one test, subdued ochre order buttons beat red by 27 percent; in direct mail, print the order card on stock in a different color from the outer envelope and letter — canary yellow and robin's egg blue are favorites.
caveats: The 20 percent abandonment-per-field figure and the 27 percent button-color result come from cited third-party and single-test sources; re-verify against your own traffic.
Color preferences are context-dependent — the source calls the ochre-over-red result surprising.

cards.title: Expect losing tests and run more of them
cards.summary: Even the best baseball team loses four in ten games; direct marketers should expect under-performance and test often enough to find winners.
cards.use_when: Setting expectations for a testing program or deciding whether to abandon direct marketing after a failed campaign
steps: Accept the source's baseball analogy: the best record in Major League Baseball still lost four of every ten games, so a percentage of test campaigns under-performing the control or losing money is normal.
Experienced direct marketers accept this because finding one winner in every two, three, or even five tests can be highly profitable.
Avoid the small-business trap of testing once every few years and then declaring that direct marketing does not work if the first attempt fails.
Do more testing of offers, reply elements, copy, and prices than you currently do.

Quantify the cost of not testing: a single promotion for a new product has roughly a 10 percent success rate in the source's framing, so a one-shot launch is about 10-to-1 against you; a .250 hitter with one at-bat has only a one in four chance of getting on base.
Put propositions to a statistically valid A/B split rather than settling them by judgment around a conference table.
caveats: The 10 percent launch-success rate is the author's estimate, not a measured industry constant.
Volume testing requires enough list or traffic size for a valid split.

cards.title: Run offer A/B splits and match landing page to ad
cards.summary: Split traffic between two offers or headlines with separate URLs, keep the landing page headline consistent with the ad, and let data pick the winner.
cards.use_when: Choosing between two offers, headlines, prices, or page variants when you cannot decide subjectively
steps: If you are mailing 5,000 postcards and cannot choose between two headlines, split the mailing in half rather than picking one — choosing subjectively gives a 50 percent chance of selecting the wrong appeal.
Drive each version to a different URL so you can measure click-through and conversion rates and see which generates the most leads.
Match the landing page headline to the ad headline, especially on the web, so the prospect knows they arrived in the right place.
When a landing page converts poorly, do not abandon the product — test different headlines, visuals, pricing, bonuses, guarantees, subheads, and copy leads, then fold the winners into the page.
Follow Peter Betuel's principle in the source: what matters is not what you think, like, believe, or prefer but what your prospects think, like, believe, and prefer.

Expect surprises. A car-rental-by-the-week company tested a free upgrade (A) against a rental discount tied to buying multiple weeks in advance with a book of tickets (B); offer B won by a wide margin with nearly a tenfold revenue increase.
caveats: The rental-company result is one case study, not a prediction for your offer.
Clean A/B reads require enough traffic or list size per cell and one changed variable at a time.

cards.title: Match the promo headline to the landing page for split tests
cards.summary: When testing headlines via ads or postcards, carry the same headline onto the landing page and use a unique URL per version for clean measurement.
cards.use_when: Running a split test across an ad, postcard, or email that sends traffic to a landing page
steps: Split the traffic source itself, not just the destination — half the postcards carry 'Tastes Great,' half carry 'Less Filling.'
Give each version its own URL so click-through and conversion rates can be attributed correctly.
Ensure the landing page headline matches the headline used in the ad or postcard that produced the click.
Then watch which version pulls slightly better and begin incorporating the winning elements into the page.
On the web this is fast and inexpensive relative to offline testing, which is why the source recommends iterating landing pages rather than giving up on a poorly converting product.
caveats: Mismatched headline and page is called out by the source as a specific risk in this type of test.
Small samples can produce noise — do not act on a slight difference without enough volume.

cards.title: Premium and guarantee offer summary: what to default to and how to test it
cards.summary: The source's closing synthesis: word and present offers prominently, expect 10–900 percent response lifts, and default to related premiums, 60–90 day unconditional guarantees, and urgency.
cards.use_when: Building or auditing a complete offer: premium, guarantee, urgency, and risk reversal
steps: Treat wording and presentation as tremendously important — the right offer can boost response rates by 10 to 900 percent according to the source, and stressing the offer in copy generates more leads and orders.
Use a premium (a free gift with order or inquiry) as the easiest way to increase response, and favor free information such as a special report, CD, or video.
Make guarantees at least 60 days and preferably 90 days, and keep them unconditional — return the product, get your money back.
Create urgency by giving the prospect a deadline or other incentive to respond now rather than later.
Design the offer so all the risk sits on the seller rather than the buyer; make buying entirely risk-free.
Test prices and terms rather than intuiting them — the source reports that the lower price is frequently not the winner.
Accept that no one can predict which offer will respond best; only a series of A/B split tests will find the winning offer for your product or service.
caveats: The 10–900 percent range is the author's broad experience claim, not a guaranteed outcome.
Longer unconditional guarantees can raise refund rates — the source does not address this trade-off.
The preference for 90 days over shorter terms is the source's recommendation; test it against your margin and return behavior.

cards.title: Use a related premium as the easy default for lead generation
cards.summary: Free booklets, reports, and product-related gifts raise response volume while attracting more qualified leads than unrelated high-value giveaways.
cards.use_when: Choosing a lead magnet or inquiry incentive for a campaign
steps: Default to a free booklet or report related to the product or service — the source says this is his personal favorite and is most often used in a soft offer ('Send for free report').

Expect modest, directly related premiums to increase total responses and deliver a greater volume of qualified leads from good prospects, even though serial freebie seekers will always respond to anything free.
Avoid unrelated high-value premiums in lead generation because they bring in large numbers of freebie seekers and other unqualified leads.
You can tie the free report to a harder next step, as when a report is promised only if a salesperson hand-delivers it — which converts a soft offer into a qualified appointment.
Remember the B2B adjustment: if the buyer is a corporate employee, a discount or company-relevant premium may outperform a personal-use gift.
caveats: The preference for related premiums is stated as the author's experience, not a tested rule.
Some freebie responses are unavoidable and should be planned for in lead-scoring and follow-up.

In business-to-business marketing, the corporate employee increasingly looks good to management by being a sharp buyer. That means getting the product at the lowest price possible. A larger discount might therefore work better than a free gift intended for personal use. If you do offer a premium to a business buyer, especially one working in a corporate setting, consider making it something related to the product and of value to the buyer’s company. For instance, a publisher selling highpriced technical journals and information databases on CD-ROM offered a free CD-ROM stacker and reader with the purchase of a group of its highpriced CD-ROM—based information products. The premium had high perceived value, was closely related to the product, and made the prospect look like a smart buyer. For lead generation, I think the best use of a premium is to offer something directly related to the product or service. My experience is that unrelated premiums of high value bring in large numbers of “freebie seekers” and other unqualified leads.

 Modest premiums that are directly related to the product or service increase the total number of responses. While you will always get some inquiries from those people who seem to send for anything and everything that’s free, you will also get a greater volume of qualified leads from good prospects. I personally like the offer of a free booklet or report related to the product or service. This is most often used in the soft offer (“Send for free report”), but it could conceivably be tied to a hard offer. For instance, you can offer an impressive report with the condition that it will be handdelivered by a salesperson. Ricoh did this many years ago when selling fax machines, copiers, and other office equipment via direct mail. You would get a little gift as an incentive for replying to the mailing. Ricoh would call to set up a time for a sales rep to come to your office and demonstrate the machine. The gift item was delivered personally by the sales rep, and you got it only after the demonstration. Samplings, Trial Offers, and Product Evaluations Are All Great Offers Three additional incentives you can use in your marketing are samples, trial offers, and product evaluations: Samples. You offer to render your service or allow the customer to use your product on a sample basis. This may be for purposes of demonstrating your service or product or for analyzing the customer’s needs to determine which of your services or products is right for them. For example, a company selling equipment that turns chemical powders into pellets says in its sales letter, “Send us a five-pound bag of your compound and tell us what size pellets you want. We will run it through our pelletizer and return it to show you the quality of the pellets it can produce.” Graver Chemical makes a similar offer for Ecosorb, a carbon-based filtration medium for purifying water supplies. Their letter states: “Is Ecosorb right for your application? We’d be delighted to evaluate a water sample to see if Ecosorb can handle your particular requirements.” Another company, a computer firm, sells a software program that businesses can use to quickly create customized applications that work with their databases. One potential buyer was skeptical and asked, “How long would it take to develop a so-and-so application for our database using your product?” Instead of answering, the software firm’s rep sat at the computer, started pressing keys, and had the application prototyped and working with the database within 30 minutes. The prospect’s response? “Decision made! We’re buying it!” Trial offers. A trial offer allows the prospect to use your product or service for a specified period at no cost and with no obligation to buy. The pelletizer manufacturer’s letter went on to say that if the sample pellets were satisfactory, they would ship a pelletizer to the prospect’s plant and let them us it for a month with no obligation. Then the company would have the option of sending it back (at the manufacturer’s expense) or buying it. A trial offer can also work with a service. If you have an online database, a long-distance telephone service, or another service where users are billed by the hour, you could offer “30 minutes of use free.” In his book Profitable Direct Marketing, Jim Kobs shows two ads from MCI. The first offers $5 off the prospect’s long-distance phone bill. The second offers 30 free minutes of long-distance calls. The “30 free minutes” offer pulled roughly twice the response of “$5 off” because customers perceived 30 free minutes of long-distance calling to be the greater value. The 30 minutes of free service is, in essence, a free trial of the long-distance phone service. Product evaluations. Similar to the free trial is the product evaluation. The gist of this offer is: “Let us send you the product at no cost, and you can perform whatever technical evaluation is required to help you decide whether it is the right product for you. If it is not, send it back and owe us nothing. If it is, you can buy it for the list price of $X.” One problem with free trials and evaluations is that prospects send for the product — and then, because of inertia, laziness, or lack of time, they don’t do anything with it. One way to overcome this problem is to combine the free trial or evaluation with an incentive to make a buying decision within a specified period of time. For instance: “If you accept our free trial offer and then decide to invest in the so-and-so system within the next 30 days, you will get 10 percent off the regular purchase price.” Mention of this time-limited offer in your ad or mailing can increase overall response. Periodic reminders to prospects via mail or phone during the evaluation period can help get more of them to try the product and increase the conversion rate of leads to sales. Creating Urgency With a Loss Leader Strategy Have you ever read an ad offering a product at a price so low that it seems impossible for the seller to be making a profit? Any item sold at or below cost to attract new customers is called a loss leader. Retail and mail order merchants sell items at or below cost to entice you to their store or get you to place an order. (Retailers refer to these discounted items as “door busters,” because they can whip consumers into such a frenzy that they will literally bust down the door to the store to get one.) Once you purchase the loss leader or door buster, you have made the transition from shopper to paying customer. And the merchant makes his profit by selling existing customers like you additional products with a regular mark-up. An example is mail order coin dealers who offer, say, an American Silver Eagle for $19.95, which they say is “our cost.” They might get 10,000 first-time customers to order the Silver Eagle. With the coin, they send out literature advertising a set of silver coins for $200. Of the initial 10,000 first-time customers, 1,000 buy the set of silver coins, generating $200,000 in revenues. Well, the same loss leader strategy that merchants have been using off line for decades to build their customer lists can now be profitably applied online. Here’s how it works. First, create your loss leader. If you are an online information marketer, it could be an e-book. This e-book should have wide appeal for all segments of your market. The topic should be one that all your customers will find interesting enough to make them want to own the e-book. And be sure it is a truly valuable product. No matter what your intent is, you always want to give your customers great value for their money. That way, they’ll come back to you for more information again and again. Assign a $39 list price to the e-book, for reasons I will make clear in minute. Next, approach your affiliates — other online marketers that you have a commission agreement with — and suggest that they sell your $39 e-book to people on their lists for $19, giving them a special $20 discount offer. Tell your affiliates that you won’t pay the customary 50 percent commission. Instead you’ll give them 100 percent commission for every book that’s sold. That’s right. They get all the money. Reason: If you give them the usual 50 percent commission on the $19 sale, their cut would be only $9.50 — too little to interest them. But 100 percent commission on a $19 sale is equivalent to a 50 percent commission on a $38 sale. And the fact that you are giving them all the commission makes them stand up and take notice. This is why I suggested assigning a retail price of $39 to the e-book. It allows you to offer the consumer a $20 discount, which has strong appeal, and still give the affiliate a $19 commission per sale, which also has strong appeal. What you end up with is a win, win, win situation. The customer gets a great $39 product for $19. The affiliate gets 100 percent of the sales. And you get a valuable list of subscribers. Where to Feature the Offer in Your Copy The offer must be featured prominently on the response device. (In Chapter 9, I will give you copy and graphics guidelines for creating winning reply elements that highlight the strong offers you build.) Of course, the offer is usually mentioned elsewhere in the copy, too. For an offer that is strong but standard, we typically write copy describing it in the closing section of the promotion. The more compelling or unusual the offer is, the more prominently you should feature it. A mailing for the McGraw-Hill Chemical Engineer’s Book Club featured an unusually generous offer: a free copy of Perry’s Handbook, a large and expensive reference book. The buyer paid only a nominal fee plus shipping and handling to get the handbook, and in exchange was enrolled in the club with a commitment to buy a few additional books. The publisher felt the handbook was such an attractive incentive that they featured it on the outer envelope of the promotion with this teaser: “Why are we giving away this 50th Anniversary Edition of Perry’s Handbook practically for free?” An advertisement for an application development tool used by programmers used the headline: “Develop applications up to 6X faster — guaranteed or your money back.” Putting the guarantee in the headline helps address skepticism for a big promise right up front. OceanofPDF.com 9 How to Write and Design Reply Elements That Flood Your Mailbox With Orders One of the most labor-intensive, time-consuming marketing tasks is copywriting. Not necessarily writing the copy … but agonizing over what has been written. As a copywriter, I do this all the time. I fret to an insane degree over every sentence, reading the copy over and over again, questioning whether the wording could be stronger. Many marketers do the same thing. They mark change after change on a nearly finished promotion, worrying about whether the copy says exactly the right thing, in exactly the right way. The irony, of course, is that in most situations, all this suffering is for naught. I don’t mean to say that copy is unimportant. But most of the time, the changes we make — punctuation, grammar, spelling, and minor word choice (e.g., whether to use “the” or “a”) — are so insignificant, it wouldn’t make one iota of difference in response whether we went with “version A” or “version B.” That said, I do think you should put in the time to carefully fine-tune your promotion … but only a small fraction of it. Specifically, here are the three “hot spots” in your promotion where what you say — and how you say it — really, really matters: The first critical portion of the copy is determined by its position in the promotion. The most important copy in a #10 direct-mail package is the outer envelope teaser — and the headline and lead of the sales letter. In a magalog, it’s the front cover … the inside front cover … the headline and lead … and the back cover. On a landing page, it’s the banner, headline, salutation, and lead. In an e-mail, it’s the subject line and the first paragraph. These sections are worth agonizing over, because different wording can result in dramatic increases or decreases in your response rates. Given the importance of the headline, should it focus on the offer instead of the product or the prospect? Do we present our offer on the front cover of a self-mailer or in the lead of a sales letter? Not usually. But if the offer is particularly powerful or unusual, then yes, you might lead with that. Here’s how I did it with a letter I used to promote my online copywriting services to a couple of hundred newsletter publishers. (It generated a 3 percent response.) _____________________________ Dear Fellow SIPA Member: A proven process for selling thousands of new subscriptions entirely over the Internet … at a tiny fraction of the cost of direct mail … … is described in a new, informative Mini-Report, “7 Steps to Selling More Newsletter Subscriptions Online.” It is yours FREE, with my compliments, when you complete and mail the card enclosed. In our new FREE special report, you’ll discover how to: ** Adapt the “Agora Model” to increase online subscription sales while slashing your marketing costs. ** Build a large and profitable opt-in e-list with a “free-onfree name-squeeze page.” ** Find the right balance of content to promotion in your email marketing — and the optimal frequency of e-mail distribution. ** Maximize conversion of “freebie seekers” to paying customers within 90 days of acquiring new online names. ** And many other ideas for boosting your online clicks, conversion rates, orders, and revenues. For nearly 3 decades, I’ve helped dozens of newsletter, book, magazine, and software publishers beat their controls — and increase their revenues — online and offline. “In one test, your promotion actually had a 14% conversion to sale,” says David Galland of Casey Research. “You can’t ask for much better than that.” But a landing page I wrote for an e-book recently generated a conversion rate of 32%. To get your FREE Online Marketing Report … free facts on my copywriting services … and samples of successful promotions I’ve written for Phillips, KCI, Weiss Research, Agora Publishing, Brownstone, Medical Economics, Ken Roberts, and other clients, just check “Copywriting Information Kit” on the enclosed reply card — and mail it today. No obligation, of course. Sincerely, Bob Bly P.S. To get an immediate cost estimate for a copywriting project, call me today at 201-385-1220. The quote is free. And there’s no commitment of any kind. _____________________________ The second critical area is the copy describing the central message, theme, or idea of your selling proposition. For instance, do you position your newsletter on energy stocks as a way for your reader to hedge his portfolio against a bear market triggered by rising oil prices? Or do you talk about how he can profit from the “next big thing” in energy investing — which, according to your editor, is that crude oil will reach $200 a barrel by the end of the decade? The “big idea” of your promotion — and the way you express it — really matters. The third critical area is the copy in the offer — specifically, how the offer is expressed on the reply element. Offering a “free information kit,” for instance, usually generates more leads than the vaguer “send for more information” — the idea of a “kit” somehow being more tangible and valuable. On the order form, changing even one word in the copy — if changing that word results in changing the offer itself — can mean the difference between a winner and a disaster. For instance, “$100 a year” vs. “$500 a year” or “10-day money-back guarantee” vs. “90-day money-back guarantee.” It is worth your time to keep polishing your headlines, leads, offer copy, theme, and big idea until you finally feel confident that what you’ve written can work. For my money, the final step in creating an irresistible offer is creating an irresistible order device. By “order device,” I mean the mechanism through which you present the offer to the prospect and with which he responds. The simplest order device, used in lead-generating direct mail, is the reply card. (You can require your prospects to affix their own postage, or you can use a prepaid business reply card.) Or you can tell the prospect to keep it as a record of his order, leaving space for him to fill in the date of the order and his check number. The tear-off stub can also highlight the guarantee. Another variation is to create an 8 1/2 x 11 inch order form. The bottom third is a tear-off business reply card (for a bill-me offer) or order card (for a mail order offer). The top two-thirds (both front and back) give the copywriter and designer additional space for selling copy: A growing number of marketers are omitting the reply card from their lead-generating direct-mail promotions. They reason that, in the Internet Age, prospects would rather reply online or call. I disagree. You should still enclose a reply card in your mailings, even if, in fact, the majority of prospects don’t use it. Reason: The reply card graphically signals to the prospect that he is supposed to reply to the mailing. Enclosing a business reply card with your sales letter actually lifts total response, including responses by phone and online, not just responses by snail mail. Years ago, a large percentage of direct-response space ads, both for mail order and lead generation, had response coupons. These days, reply coupons in print ads are a rarity. I still like them, though, for the same reason I like business reply cards in direct mail: They tell the prospect: “Hey, this is one of those ads you are supposed to respond to — and if you do, you get something.” In my experience, adding a reply coupon to a space ad increases response by approximately 10 to 15 percent. The reply coupon appears in the bottom right corner of the ad. In your insertion order, you require the ad to be placed on a right-hand page so the coupon is easy to clip out, as in this classic ad for Dale Carnegie’s book, How to Win Friends and Influence People : Do not assume that your prospects will always prefer to contact you by phone or online. Your order device should offer multiple response options, including: Mail back the reply element. Fax back the reply element. Order or request more information on the Web. Reply via e-mail. Call a toll-free phone number. For direct mail written to generate an order, the response mechanism is usually an order card or form. A #9 business reply envelope (BRE) is included so the recipient can return the order form with his payment. For years, the standard reply element in a #10 direct-mail package was a 4 x 9 inch order card, which the recipient placed with payment in the BRE without folding it. Today, many marketers are switching to an 8 1/2 x 11 inch order form that folds like a letter for placement into the BRE. The larger order form has space for more copy. One popular style is to make the order form resemble an invoice on which all the features or benefits of the product are listed as separate “items,” with a price or value for each one. This creates the perception that the prospect is getting a lot for her money. Others prefer cleanly designed order forms that are easy to fill out. With membership, mortgage, insurance, and other offers where the prospect is applying for a service he may or may not qualify for, you can design the reply elements to look like a membership application or official enrollment form: Often-neglected, tokens, peel-off stickers, stamp sheets, and other physical devices on the order form are a proven response-booster. With multiple products, such as magazine subscriptions, you can have a stamp sheet with the name and picture of each magazine on the sheet. The customer affixes the stamps for the magazines she wants to receive on the order form. An even more-overlooked variation is the “yes/no/maybe” offer, which may be done with or without peel-off stickers. The prospect who wants to order affixes the “yes” label to the order sheet. The prospect who is less certain can request a free trial with the “maybe” sticker. The negative offer (see Chapter 1) may be selected with the “no” sticker. You can also use “yes/no” stickers — or even just “yes.” Following are two examples: Order Devices That Increase Response Here are nine proven techniques for creating reply elements that effectively present your offer for maximum response: 1. Show a picture of the premium. If you are giving away merchandise, show a photo of the item you are giving away. If the premium is a free special report, show an image of the front cover. If you are giving away multiple special reports, spread their front covers out in a fanfold. 2. Highlight your guarantee on the order device. Put a certificate-style border around the guarantee. Add the signature of the company owner beneath the guarantee copy. Print the guarantee in clear, legible type. 3. Leave sufficient space on the order form for the prospect to write in his name and address. If the area is too cramped, he may give up in frustration. 4. If you want to track response with a key code on the mailing label, design your mail piece so the label is returned with the response device. This requires the mailing label to be affixed to or imprinted upon the reply element. 5. You can track phone responses without having a special phone number for each promotion. After your phone number on the order form, put something like “Ask for Betty” or “Ask for Extension 112” as a code. Your operators should ask each caller which extension or person they want. Their answer tells you which promotion they’re responding to. If you’re having people order or request more information on the Web, send traffic for each promotion to a unique URL. 6. Create domain names that are easy to remember, like www.myveryfirstebook.com or www.beer.com, which get more traffic than longer ones that do not connect logically with the product. 7. When you are using a Web-based form to generate leads, like registering for a free webinar or downloading a free white paper, it’s important to ask the minimum number of qualifying questions. Reason: The more information you require the prospect to fill in, the lower your conversion rate (the percentage of prospects who will complete the transaction). According to an article in DM News (10/20/08, p. 11), approximately 20 percent of visitors abandon the form for every field or question that is presented. So ask only what is necessary. For consumer online marketing, that’s usually just name and e-mail address. For B2B, it might include company name and phone number. If your sales process requires an inbound phone call to the lead, then collecting the phone number is mandatory. 8. Web-based forms can also be used for e-commerce or online mailorder marketing. The online order form may be the actual shopping cart order page or a custom-designed page preceding the shopping cart order page. A frequent problem with online ordering is “AVS mismatch.” The customer’s card is rejected, which irritates the customer who complains she’s using a valid card. To combat this problem, add copy to your order page reminding the reader to make sure the name they enter on the page matches exactly the name on the credit card they are using. 9. Online and offline, color can make a difference in your response rate. In one test, a marketer tested identical landing pages, with the only difference being that the order buttons on version “A” were red and on version “B” they were ochre. Surprisingly, the subdued ochre buttons outperformed red by 27 percent. And you can get a lift in direct mail by printing the order card or form on a paper stock that’s a different color than the outer envelope and letter. I particularly like canary yellow or robin’s egg blue. Testing Offers and Offer Devices The Florida Marlins, with 23 wins and 14 losses, once had the best record in Major League baseball. But that means the best-performing team in professional baseball still lost four out of every 10 games it played. And remember: That was the best record in baseball at the time. What’s ironic is that businesspeople who accept this statistical fact about baseball without a second thought … absolutely go bonkers when even one of their marketing programs fails. Experienced direct marketers know — and expect — that a percentage of their test campaigns will under-perform the control or even lose money. They accept this fact without despair, because they know that if one test mailing in every two … or every three … or even every five is a winner — they can make a lot of money. Inexperienced direct marketers don’t get this, however. As a result, countless small businesses test direct-marketing offers only once every few years, making it difficult if not impossible to identify the winning offer — the one offer that can multiply their sales two, three, even fivefold or more. If they don’t hit a home run the first time at bat, they loudly proclaim that “direct marketing doesn’t work” … and abandon it wholesale. If you’re a business owner or marketing professional, is there a better way to get direct marketing to work for you? Yes. Simply do more testing — of offers, reply elements, copy, prices — than you do right now. Let’s say you are planning to mail 5,000 postcards to drive people to a Web page. You just can’t decide which of two headlines you like — “Tastes Great” vs. “Less Filling.” If you subjectively pick just one, your risk of selecting the wrong sales appeal — and, therefore, having your postcard mailing bomb — is 50 percent. A much better approach is to split the postcard mailing into two batches, half with the headline “Tastes Great” and the other half with “Less Filling.” _________________________ “Don’t let personal preferences get in the way. What’s important is not what you think, like, believe, or prefer … it’s what your prospects think, like, believe, and prefer.” — Peter Betuel _________________________ Each postcard in this test drives traffic to a different URL, so you can measure the click-through and conversion rates, and then see which generates the most leads. In this type of test, it’s important for the headline on the landing page to match the headline on the postcard. Especially on the Web, testing variations — of headlines, copy, graphics, formats, and offers — is relatively quick, easy, and inexpensive. So if you create a landing page to sell a product on the Internet and your conversion rate is poor, don’t give up on the product. Instead, test different headlines, visuals, pricing, bonuses, guarantees, subheads, and copy leads. You’ll notice that one headline pulls slightly better than another … or one price generates more orders. Start incorporating the winners of those tests into your landing page, and in no time flat, you can take the promotion from marginally profitable to a real winner — all courtesy of testing. I am amazed at how many marketers, large and small, online and offline, invest significant sums in developing products — and then promote each product with just a single promotion … with no testing of any kind. If you are doing this, you are essentially hoping you’ll get a hit with only once chance at bat. In baseball, a .250 hitter who gets only one at-bat has a one in four chance of getting on base. In reality, for product launches, the success rate is often as low as 10 percent — which means that a single promotion has only a one in 10 chance of making money. That makes the odds of winning with a one-shot promotion 10 to one against you. _________________________ “Advertising arguments should only be settled by testing, not arguments around a conference table.” — Claude Hopkins _________________________ By testing different copy, offers, designs, and formats, you can significantly tip those odds in your favor. Giving your marketing multiple chances to score a winner is clearly the way to go. Copywriter Peter Betuel advises marketers: Don’t let personal preferences get in the way. What’s important is not what you think, like, believe, or prefer … it’s what your prospects think, like, believe, and prefer. No one can predict which offer will work best, and the least effective way to make marketing decisions is through subjective judgment. But as a direct marketer, you don’t have to rely on subjective judgment. You can put almost any proposition — e.g., offer “A” vs. offer “B,” or long copy vs. short copy — to a direct test with a statistically valid A/B split. For instance, a company that rented automobiles by the week tested two offers. Offer “A” was a free upgrade to a larger size model. Offer “B” was a rental discount given in exchange for purchasing multiple weeks of rentals in advance. (Customers would get a book of tickets they could redeem at the car counter.) To almost everyone’s surprise, offer “B” outperformed offer “A” significantly, generating nearly a tenfold increase in revenues. As advertising legend Claude Hopkins once said: “Advertising arguments should only be settled by testing, not arguments around a conference table.” And that includes the answer to the question: Which offer is best? In Conclusion … The way an offer is worded and presented is tremendously important. The right offer can boost response rates by 10 to 900 percent. The more you stress your offer in your promotional copy, the more leads and orders you will generate. Testing different prices and terms can yield big improvements in sales, and the results are often surprising. For example, the lower price is frequently not the winner of the test. The easiest way to increase response rates is to offer a premium — a free gift with order or inquiry. Free information — e.g., a free special report, CD, or video — can work extremely well as a premium. Guarantees should be at least 60 and preferably 90 days, and they should be unconditional. (Return the product and you get your money back.) Create a sense of urgency by giving the prospect a deadline or other incentive to respond to your offer now instead of later. Design your offer so all the risk is on the seller’s shoulders, not the buyer’s. Make buying entirely risk-free. You can never predict which offer will get the best response. Only by doing a series of A/B split tests will you find the winning offer for your product or service.
